Semantic Zone-Based Map Management for Stable AI-Integrated
Mobile Robots
Huichang Yun and Seungho Yoo∗
Abstract— Recent advances in large AI models (VLMs and
LLMs) and joint use of the 3D dense maps, enable mobile robots
to provide more powerful and interactive services grounded
in rich spatial context. However, deploying both heavy AI
models and dense maps on edge robots is challenging under
strict memory budgets. When the memory budget is exceeded,
required keyframes may not be loaded in time, which can
degrade the stability of position estimation and interfering
model performance. We proposes a semantic zone-based map
management approach to stabilize dense-map utilization under
memory constraints. We associate keyframes with semantic
indoor regions (e.g., rooms and corridors) and keyframe man-
agement at the semantic zone level prioritizes spatially relevant
map content while respecting memory constraints. This reduces
keyframe loading and unloading frequency and memory usage.
We evaluate the proposed approach in large-scale simulated
indoor environments and on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
under concurrent SLAM–VLM execution. With Qwen3.5:0.8b,
the proposed method improves throughput by 3.3 tokens/s
and reduces latency by 21.7% relative to a geometric map-
management strategy. Furthermore, while the geometric strat-
egy suffers from out-of-memory failures and stalled execution
under memory pressure, the proposed method eliminates both
issues, preserving localization stability and enabling robust
VLM operation. These results demonstrate that the proposed
approach enables efficient dense map utilization for memory
constrained, AI-integrated mobile robots. Code is available at:
https://github.com/huichangs/rtabmap/tree/segment
I. INTRODUCTION
With recent advances in robotics and large-scale Artificial
Intelligence (AI) models, mobile robots can provide more
detailed services that are closely related to daily life. To
deliver such services within a given area, robots require
detailed information about the surrounding environment, in-
cluding persistent spatial memory and accurate localization.
To obtain this information, maps are essential, and high-
capacity 3D dense maps are commonly used in mobile
robot services. Building on this foundation, powerful models
and rich indoor context enable spatially grounded services
beyond basic navigation. These capabilities allow robots to
understand and interpret language instructions that refer to
places and objects (e.g., “Go to the table next to the sofa in
the hallway”) and execute them reliably using a consistent
3D map frame. These capabilities significantly expand what
robots can do and broaden their potential applications.
However, deploying AI models together with large 3D map
resources on robots is challenging because they operate in
more resource-constrained environments than workstations

memory limits. Even in conventional robot deployments
without AI workloads, it is difficult to load the entire map
into memory at once, so keyframes are dynamically loaded
and unloaded during operation. Under tight memory con-
straints, fine-grained keyframe retrieval consumes substantial
memory, and continual retrieval for new areas forces frequent
memory allocation and cleanup, which increases the fre-
quency of load and unload operations and system overhead.
More importantly, when available memory is insufficient,
loop closure can fail because the system cannot keep enough
keyframes in memory. As a result, loop closure outcomes
may become unstable or incorrect.
To mitigate the issues discussed above, we propose a
semantic zone-based map management approach that enables
stable 3D dense map utilization under strict memory con-
straints. Since typical mobile robot motion is continuous in
space and time, the system can anticipate which regions are
likely to be needed and use this to load map information
more effectively. Given the continuity of robot motion, likely
travel directions and forthcoming locations can be estimated,
allowing keyframes to be prefetched only for zones expected
to be relevant. Also, eviction of keyframes is likewise guided
by zone prediction. With this approach, the robot can effec-
tively use its limited memory by combining prediction-based
zone eviction with zone-level batch loading and unloading of
keyframes, preventing memory saturation. Figure 1 illustrates
the proposed mechanism. Figure 1a shows the environment
partitioned into semantic zones and the robot’s planned route,
which provides the basis for predicting likely upcoming
zones. Figure 1b then depicts how only a subset of zones
is activated around the robot’s progress, enabling zone-level
batch load and unload of keyframes while respecting the
memory limit.
To realize and validate our proposed approach in large-
scale indoor environments, we built on a simulation en-
vironment with Nvidia Isaac simulation, and implemented
our proposed methods on Jetson Orin Nano[1], which has
8 GB of unified memory, with concurrent execution of
VLM models (Gemma[2] and Qwen[3]), and RTAB-Map[4].
With the evaluation result, our proposed approach, semantic
zone-based keyframe management, could provide a prac-
tical mechanism to improve the robustness of dense map
utilization on memory-constrained AI-integrated robots. The
contribution of our paper is as follows:
•We motivate dense map utilization as a key enabler
of spatially grounded, high-quality robot services when
combined with large AI models, and identify memoryarXiv:2603.29627v1  [cs.RO]  31 Mar 2026

II. RELATED WORK
In this section we review prior research on memory-
efficient map and keyframe management, semantic and topo-
logical representations for scalable SLAM, and systems that
balance accuracy with resource constraints. And we sum-
marize how these strands motivate our zone-based approach
and clarify the gap addressed by prediction-guided memory
regulation.
A. Memory-Efficient and Scalable Map/Keyframe Manage-
ment in SLAM
Map growth and increasing memory demand are long-
standing bottlenecks in large-scale and long-term SLAM.
Prior work has pursued memory efficiency either by reduc-
ing map size—through pruning, sparsification, or selective
keyframe retention—or by preserving map content while
constraining only theresidentworking set. Representative
examples of the former include information-theoretic prun-
ing for compressing pose graphs [5], sliding-window map
sparsification [6], and optimization-based keyframe selec-
tion to reduce redundancy under map-size constraints [7].
While effective for bounding resources, these approaches
may discard map elements that could be useful when the
robot revisits areas or when downstream modules require
rich spatial context.
Motivated by the growing value of co-executing large
AI models (e.g., VLMs) with 3D dense maps for context-
grounded robot services, we focus on map-preserving mem-
ory management that maintains map quality while limiting
in-memory usage. RTAB-Map exemplifies this direction by
providing database-backed hierarchical memory and explicit
keyframe load/unload mechanisms for long-term operationunder bounded resources [8], [9], [10], [4]. Complementary
scalability techniques further structure maps into higher-
level units, such as hierarchical or topological representations
and submaps, to localize optimization and restrict search to
spatially relevant portions [11], [12], [13], [14]. Resource-
constrained deployment has also motivated adaptive and
hardware-aware SLAM designs that explicitly account for
limited compute and memory budgets [15], [16].
However, these works typically decide what to retain
or activate using geometric, temporal, or graph-structural
cues, and region/submap structures are primarily introduced
for scalability of optimization or retrieval rather than for
memory-bounded runtime activation in the presence of com-
peting workloads. In contrast, our work applies semantic
information directly to map management, partitioning space
into semantically meaningful zones to enable more efficient
map activation and memory use.
B. Semantic Information for SLAM and Robot Map Utiliza-
tion
Semantic information has been widely integrated into
SLAM to enhance robustness and scene understanding, in-
cluding segment-based localization and semantic cues for
handling dynamic environments [17], [18], [19]. Recent
surveys highlight a growing emphasis on semantic under-
standing and open-world robustness, and hierarchical se-
mantic representations have been explored for large-scale
reasoning [20], [21]. With the rise of large visual models,
early systems incorporate foundation-model perception into
SLAM pipelines, and recent work investigates VLM-driven
keyframe selection to reduce redundancy [22], [23].
Despite this progress, most semantic SLAM efforts fo-
cus on perception quality, localization robustness, or map
representation. Our work instead leverages semantic zones
to regulate runtime keyframe load/unload under memory
constraints, improving stability when dense maps and heavy
AI models are co-executed on edge platforms.

III. SEMANTIC ZONE-BASED MAP
MANAGEMENT
Robots equipped with large-scale AI models and 3D
dense maps can deliver increasingly diverse and high-quality
services. However, in mobile robotic platforms with limited
hardware resources, it is not feasible to retain all keyframes
stored in the map database in memory simultaneously. As a
result, keyframes should be loaded from and unloaded to the
map database during runtime.
Conventional systems typically perform load and unload
operations based on recency or geometric proximity. Under
memory-constrained conditions, however, repeated database
access and fine-grained keyframe retrieval can significantly
increase the frequency of load and unload operations, im-
posing substantial overhead on the system. In extreme cases,
delayed keyframe loading may destabilize loop closure exe-
cution, leading to degraded localization performance.
To address this issue, we propose a semantic zone-
based map management approach. Instead of accessing
keyframes individually across the entire map, we associate
each keyframe with a predefined semantic zone (e.g., rooms,
corridors) and perform keyframe management at the zone
granularity. By enforcing strict zone-level control and main-
taining the number of active keyframes within a predefined
memory threshold, the proposed approach stabilizes memory
usage and improves the robustness of map utilization.
Figure 2 illustrates an overview of the proposed semantic
zone-based map management.
A. Semantic Zones
We adopt semantic zones as a structural unit for map
management. A semantic zone corresponds to a spatially
meaningful region, such as a room or corridor. Fig 1a
illustrates an example of semantic zone partitioning in the
hospital environment.The motivation for applying semantic zones arises from
the spatial characteristics of service robot operation. Robots
typically interact with the environment based on functional
regions rather than arbitrary geometric partitions. For in-
stance, when a robot navigates along a corridor, it primarily
requires map information associated with that corridor; de-
tailed structure inside adjacent rooms is often irrelevant to
the current task, even if those rooms are physically close.
This suggests that map utilization naturally follows semantic
boundaries.
Maintaining keyframes from spatially or functionally un-
related zones in memory can increase retrieval overhead
and memory pressure without contributing to localization or
loop closure performance. Organizing keyframes according
to semantic zones therefore enables memory management
that aligns with the robot’s spatial usage patterns and task
relevance.
Formally, we assume that the environment is partitioned
into a finite set of semantic zones,Z={z 1,z2,...,z K}.
The proposed method does not depend on how these zones
are generated; it only assumes that each keyframe can be
associated with one of the predefined regions.
Lets idenote a keyframe stored in the map database. Each
keyframe is assigned to a semantic zone according to its
spatial location:z(s i)∈Z. For each zonez∈Z, we define
the corresponding keyframe set asS z={s i|z(s i) =z}. This
zone-to-keyframe organization will be used in the following
subsection to define which keyframes are retained in memory
at runtime.
B. Semantic Zone Based Keyframe Management
Figure 2 illustrates the proposed runtime keyframe man-
agement. Given the current estimated pose, the Semantic
Zone Manager determines the current semantic zone and
updates the set of zones that should be active. Based on this
decision, it forms an active keyframe list, which specifies

which keyframes should be available for localization and
loop closure. The active keyframe list is used to retrieve the
corresponding keyframes from the map database.
In parallel, the Memory Manager strictly enforces the
memory limit (MemoryThr) by controlling which zones
remain loaded in memory. We define the set of zones
currently retained in memory as the active zone set,A t⊆Z,
which corresponds to theActive Zone Listin Figure 2. The
active keyframes retained in memory are then

IV. IMPLEMENTATION
We adopt RTAB-Map as the baseline SLAM system for
implementing our map-management approach, and we use its
default keyframe retrieval and memory-management behav-
ior as the baseline strategy. Many SLAM frameworks control
map growth through pruning or culling, or through sliding-
window optimization, thereby reducing resident memory by
discarding map elements rather than swapping them between
long-term storage and a bounded working set. In con-
trast, RTAB-Map provides a hierarchical memory structure
consisting of working, short-term, and long-term memory,
with explicit mechanisms to unload keyframes from active
memory and reload them from the on-disk database when
revisiting previously mapped areas. RTAB-Map’s default
load and unload decisions are primarily driven by geometric
proximity and pose-graph structure, making it a natural
geometric baseline for evaluating the benefit of semantic
zone–based map management under an otherwise identical
SLAM pipeline. These properties make RTAB-Map well

We integrate the proposed method by modifying RTAB-
Map’s memory-management pipeline only. We reuse RTAB-
Map’s built-in keyframe load and unload interfaces to
manage the in-memory working set, while keeping pose
estimation, loop-closure detection, and graph optimization
unchanged.
During the offline phase, we assign a semantic zone label
to each stored keyframe and persist it as lightweight metadata
indexed by the keyframe ID. We maintain a mapping from
keyframe ID to zone for fast lookup and, for each zone, a
list of keyframe IDs belonging to that zone, enabling zone-
granularity load and unload operations.
During online localization, after RTAB-Map updates the
pose estimate for each incoming sensor update, we determine
the zone corresponding to the current pose. A zone-transition
event triggers a memory update. When a zone is activated, we
load all keyframes assigned to that zone from the database
into active memory. When a zone is evicted, we unload all
keyframes in that zone, preserving them in the database while
removing them from the in-memory working set. Issuing
load and unload at zone granularity reduces the number of
database transactions compared to fine-grained per-keyframe
retrieval.
We enforce a strict memory budget using a keyframe-
capacity threshold, denotedMemoryThr, which specifies
the maximum number of resident keyframes. Before ac-
tivating a new zone, we predict the number of resident
keyframes using only zone-level counts from the metadata.
If the prediction exceedsMemoryThr, we iteratively evict
zones according to a zone-level least-recently-used policy
and unload their keyframes until the constraint is satisfied.
We then load the requested zone, ensuring that memory usage
does not temporarily exceed the budget.
Once loaded, keyframes are consumed by RTAB-Map’s

localization and loop-closure modules through the standard
processing flow. Thus, our implementation controls which
keyframes are resident at runtime, while RTAB-Map’s origi-
nal procedures, including loop-closure verification and graph
optimization, operate normally on the currently loaded sub-
set.
V. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
We conducted experiments to evaluate the proposed se-
mantic zone based memory management approach and an-
alyze the impact of utilizing VLM and maps in an edge
resource environment. The objectives of these experiments
were to determine how the proposed semantic region-based
map management approach improves memory performance
during dense map operations and whether these memory
improvements impact the performance of AI models such as
VLM. Specifically, we evaluate (i) the reduction in memory
footprint and load/unload churn achieved by semantic zone
based keyframe management, and (ii) the resulting impact
on concurrent SLAM–VLM execution.
A. Test Environments
Experiments were conducted in large-scale indoor en-
vironments built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, including a hos-
pital scenario. Localization was performed using a pre-
built 3D dense map, and online map updates were disabled
during evaluation to isolate the effects of runtime map
utilization and memory regulation. Semantic zones were
manually defined to partition the environment into spatially
meaningful indoor regions (e.g., rooms and corridors), and
keyframes in the map database were associated with these
zones. Unless otherwise noted,Basicdenotes the default
RTAB-Map keyframe loading/unloading mechanism, while
Semanticrefers to our semantic zone-based map management
strategy.
All experiments were executed on an NVIDIA Jetson
Orin Nano with 8GB unified memory to emulate resource-
constrained edge deployment. We attemptqwen3:2b/4b,
qwen3.5:0.8b/2b, gemma3:4bas the VLM workload
because it represents a deployable edge-scale model while
still imposing substantial memory pressure on an 8GB plat-
form. In our setup, the model runs concurrently with SLAM
and tends to consume most available memory during infer-
ence, making it suitable for stress-testing memory contention.

In the basic algorithm, enabling VLM reduces the update
rate from 0.96 Hz to 0.65 Hz and decreases the number
of accepted loop closures from 53 to 31. The mean total
processing time also increases sharply from 779.41 ms to
5064.87 ms. This runtime slowdown is accompanied by clear

from 0.20 m to 0.42 m, and rotational RPE RMSE increases
from 0.38◦to 1.00◦. These results indicate that the basic
memory-management configuration is strongly affected by
concurrent VLM execution, which reduces loop-closure op-
portunities and significantly degrades trajectory quality.
Figure 4 shows a trajectory comparison between GT, the
baseline configuration, baseline+VLM, and semantic+VLM.
The final approved loop closure occurs at the location
indicated by the blue circle, and no further loop closures
are approved until the scenario ends. This indicates that the
baseline algorithm failed to properly perform loop closure
due to insufficient memory, preventing keyframes from being
loaded in time.
In contrast, the semantic zone based memory management
exhibits much more stable performance under the same
concurrent execution conditions. Enabling VLM only slightly
increases the update rate from 0.96 Hz to 0.95 Hz, and the
average total processing time increases from 566.06 ms to
784.81 ms. However, this increase is much smaller than the
increase observed in the baseline algorithm, and the perfor-
mance difference is also much smaller. Overall, these results
show that semantic zone memory management supporting
more robust dense-map utilization under concurrent edge-AI
workloads.
D. Impact of Concurrent SLAM-VLM Execution on VLM
Performance
To validate and evaluate the operational effectiveness of
our proposed approach, we visualized the VLM inference
metrics, Token Generation Speed and End-to-End Latency,
spatially over the robot’s physical path with Figure 5, 6, and
7. A direct comparison between two configurations, Basic +
VLM (baseline) and Semantic + VLM (proposed), reveals
distinct pipeline characteristics. The baseline configure ran
VLM with the default SLAM configuration, which uses
a conventional keyframe retrieval scheme. And the other
experiment, proposed, ran VLM with our semantic zone
based approach, which acquires keyframes based on semanticzone information. Among the two experiments, the VLM
operates under identical inference conditions.
The baseline case frequently experiences severe latency
spikes, which presented with annotated by the brighter,
resulting in a token generation rate of 14.35 tokens/s with an
average latency of 12.93 seconds. These performance drops
typically align with complex regions of the environment
where dense, unfiltered visual data overwhelms the VLM’s
processing capacity. Even worse, this approach fails to gen-
erate token after approximately 370 seconds of operation,
then freeze for over 142 seconds until reach to the end point
of the trajectory.
However, our proposed approach achieved robust opera-
tion and also presents better VLM metrics over baseline.
With our approach, VLM continuously generated tokens with
the average speed of 15.19 tokens/s with an average latency
of 11.68 seconds, without any freeze. Based on these results,
we were able to confirm that our proposed method could
enables VLM to produce better results in terms of token
generation speed, delay, and operational stability.
VI. DISCUSSION
We proposed a semantic zone-based map management
scheme and, which technique for efficiently utilizing memory
in memory starving environments. We demonstrated that
our proposed approach can simultaneously utilize memory-
intensive RTAB-Map and VLM models with limited memory
space. However, the following considerations must be con-
sidered.
During our experiments, we observed that when the
memory limit is reached, additional keyframes cannot be
loaded into memory from the map database. This restriction
may delay or prevent keyframe retrieval required for loop
closure, ultimately causing loop closure failure despite the
availability of correct correspondences in the database. Such
behavior highlights that memory saturation is not merely a
performance issue but can directly affect localization stability
in edge environments.
Several limitations remain. First, semantic zones were
manually defined in the current study. Using an automated or
adaptive spatial segmentation strategies may further improve
scalability and reduce manual configuration effort. Second,
the eviction policy was based on a least recently used (LRU)
rule. More advanced strategies that incorporate task context,
robot trajectory prediction, or semantic importance may yield
improved keyframe selection efficiency.

Future work may explore dynamic zone refinement, se-
mantic importance weighting, and integration with online
map updates. Additionally, more systematic evaluation of
retrieval hit ratio and long-term deployment stability would
further clarify the benefits of semantic aware keyframe
selection under varying workload conditions.
VII. CONCLUSION
We presented a semantic zone-based map management
approach that stabilizes dense-map utilization under strict
memory constraints. By associating keyframes with semantic
zones and applying prediction-guided zone activation and
eviction, the method enforces a fixed memory budget while
preserving spatially relevant map content and reducing fre-
quent memory accesses caused by keyframe loading and
unloading. The zone-level batch operations make memory

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces a "semantic zone-based map management" approach for AI-integrated mobile robots operating under strict memory constraints. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Deploying large AI models (VLMs, LLMs) and dense 3D maps on memory-limited edge robots leads to challenges in loading necessary keyframes, degrading position estimation stability and AI model performance.
*   **Proposed Solution:** A semantic zone-based map management system that associates keyframes with indoor semantic regions (e.g., rooms, corridors). This approach prioritizes spatially relevant map content at the semantic zone level, respecting memory limits.
*   **Benefits:** This method reduces the frequency of keyframe loading/unloading, decreases memory usage, and eliminates out-of-memory failures and stalled execution, thereby preserving localization stability and enabling robust VLM operation.
*   **Evaluation:** The approach was evaluated in large-scale simulated indoor environments and on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, showing improvements in throughput and latency compared to a geometric map-management strategy.
*   **Contributions:** The paper highlights the importance of dense map utilization for AI-grounded robot services, identifies memory saturation as a bottleneck, proposes a semantic zone-based keyframe management mechanism, and provides an edge-oriented evaluation.
*   **Related Work:** The document also reviews existing research on memory-efficient SLAM, semantic information in SLAM, and systems balancing accuracy with resource constraints, differentiating the proposed approach by its direct use of semantic zones for runtime memory regulation.

nodes.title: Semantic Information for SLAM and Robot Map Utilization
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a semantic zone-based approach to map management for robots, particularly in scenarios involving large-scale AI models and limited memory resources. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Large-scale SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) and the co-execution of large AI models (like VLMs) with 3D dense maps create significant memory saturation bottlenecks on resource-constrained robotic platforms.
*   **Proposed Solution:** A semantic zone-based keyframe load/unload mechanism that enforces a runtime memory limit. This approach partitions the environment into semantically meaningful zones (e.g., rooms, corridors) and manages keyframes at the zone granularity.
*   **Mechanism:**
    *   **Semantic Zones:** The environment is divided into predefined semantic zones, and each keyframe is associated with a specific zone.
    *   **Runtime Management:** The system determines the robot's current semantic zone based on its estimated pose. It then maintains an "active zone list" and an "unload zone list" to manage which keyframes are loaded into memory, ensuring compliance with a memory threshold.
*   **Benefits:**
    *   **Memory Efficiency:** Stabilizes memory usage by aligning map utilization with the robot's spatial usage patterns and task relevance.
    *   **Robustness:** Improves the stability of map utilization and potentially loop closure execution by reducing frequent database access and fine-grained keyframe retrieval overhead.
    *   **Scalability:** Addresses the challenges of large-scale and long-term SLAM by providing a structured way to manage map data.
*   **Evaluation:** The document mentions an edge-oriented evaluation with large-scale indoor environments and concurrent VLM execution on a Jetson Orin Nano.
*   **Related Work:** The document reviews prior research in memory-efficient map/keyframe management, semantic and topological representations for SLAM, and systems balancing accuracy with resource constraints, highlighting how their proposed zone-based approach addresses gaps in existing methods.

structure.title: SEMANTIC ZONE-BASED MEMORY MANAGEMENT
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a semantic zone-based map management approach for robots, particularly those with large AI models and 3D dense maps operating in memory-constrained environments. The core problem addressed is the inefficiency and overhead of traditional keyframe loading and unloading based on recency or geometric proximity, which can degrade localization performance.

The proposed solution involves:

*   **Semantic Zones:** Partitioning the environment into meaningful regions (e.g., rooms, corridors) that align with a robot's functional interaction patterns.
*   **Zone-Granularity Management:** Instead of managing individual keyframes, the system manages keyframes at the zone level.
*   **Semantic Zone Manager:** This component uses the robot's estimated pose to identify the current semantic zone and determine which zones should be active.
*   **Memory Manager:** This component enforces a memory threshold by maintaining an active zone list and an unload zone list. It ensures that memory limits are met before loading new keyframes from the map database, thereby stabilizing memory usage and improving map utilization robustness.
*   **Active Keyframe List:** The Semantic Zone Manager generates this list based on the active zones, specifying which keyframes should be retained in memory.

nodes.title: Zone-Guided Keyframe Management
nodes.summary:
The document describes a semantic zone-based map management approach for mobile robots equipped with large AI models and 3D dense maps. The core problem addressed is the infeasibility of storing all map keyframes in memory on resource-constrained robotic platforms. The proposed solution involves organizing keyframes into semantic zones (e.g., rooms, corridors) and managing them at this zone granularity, rather than individually.

Key points covered include:

*   **Problem Statement:** Limited memory on mobile robots prevents storing all keyframes from large-scale maps, leading to performance degradation due to frequent loading/unloading.
*   **Proposed Solution:** A semantic zone-based map management system that associates keyframes with predefined semantic regions.
*   **Semantic Zones:** Spatially meaningful regions (rooms, corridors) that align with robot operational patterns and task relevance.
*   **Keyframe Management:**
    *   **Semantic Zone Manager:** Determines the current semantic zone based on the robot's estimated pose and updates the list of active zones.
    *   **Memory Manager:** Enforces a memory limit (MemoryThr) by maintaining an active zone list and an unload zone list. It ensures that memory constraints are met before loading new keyframes by evicting entire zones if necessary.
*   **Benefits:** Stabilizes memory usage, improves robustness of map utilization, reduces overhead from repeated database access, and enhances localization performance.
*   **Implementation:** The approach is implemented by modifying the memory management pipeline of the RTAB-Map SLAM system. Keyframes are assigned zone labels as metadata, and load/unload operations are performed at the zone level.
*   **Algorithm:** A detailed algorithm outlines the runtime procedure for semantic zone-based keyframe management, including zone prediction, memory constraint checking, zone eviction, and keyframe loading.

nodes.title: Prediction-Guided Zone Activation and Eviction
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a semantic zone-based keyframe management system designed to optimize memory usage for dense-map localization, particularly in shared edge resource environments. The core idea is to manage keyframes by loading and unloading them in batches based on semantic zones rather than individual keyframes.

Key points covered include:

*   **Active Zone Set:** A subset of all zones currently loaded into memory.
*   **Memory Manager:** Enforces a strict memory limit (MemoryThr) by controlling which zones remain loaded.
*   **Keyframe Capacity Prediction:** Before activating a new zone, the system predicts the total number of keyframes that would be in memory and compares it to the maximum allowed capacity (Kmax).
*   **Unload Zone Set:** If the predicted keyframe count exceeds the capacity, zones are evicted from the active set (e.g., using a least-recently-used policy) and their keyframes are unloaded.
*   **Unload-then-Load Mechanism:** This process ensures that runtime keyframe availability aligns with semantic zone relevance while strictly adhering to memory constraints.
*   **Implementation with RTAB-Map:** The proposed method is integrated into the RTAB-Map SLAM system, modifying its memory management pipeline.
*   **Offline Phase:** Semantic zone labels are assigned to keyframes and stored as metadata.
*   **Online Localization:** Zone transitions trigger memory updates, loading or unloading all keyframes associated with a zone.
*   **Zone-Granularity Operations:** Loading and unloading at the zone level reduces database transactions compared to per-keyframe operations.
*   **Strict Memory Budget Enforcement:** A keyframe-capacity threshold (MemoryThr) is used, and eviction occurs iteratively if the predicted memory usage exceeds this threshold.

structure.title: SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
structure.summary:
The document describes a semantic zone-based map management approach for robots operating with large AI models and 3D dense maps on resource-constrained platforms. The core problem addressed is the infeasibility of storing all map keyframes in memory simultaneously. The proposed solution involves:

*   **Semantic Zones:** Partitioning the environment into meaningful regions (e.g., rooms, corridors) and associating keyframes with these zones.
*   **Zone-Granularity Management:** Instead of managing keyframes individually, the system manages them at the zone level.
*   **Semantic Zone Manager:** Uses the robot's estimated pose to determine the current semantic zone and identify which zones should be active.

*   **Unload-then-Load Mechanism:** When a new zone needs to be activated and memory is limited, less relevant zones are unloaded in batch before loading the new zone's keyframes.

This leads to more stable localization and map utilization.

structure.title: EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
structure.summary:
This partial document describes an experimental evaluation of a semantic zone-based memory management approach for SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) systems, particularly in resource-constrained edge environments. The main points covered are:

*   **Implementation Details:** The proposed approach controls which keyframes are loaded at runtime, integrating with existing localization and loop-closure modules.
*   **Experimental Objectives:** To assess the memory performance improvements of the semantic zone-based approach during dense map operations and its impact on AI models like VLMs (Vision-Language Models). Specifically, it aims to measure memory footprint reduction, load/unload churn, and the effect on concurrent SLAM-VLM execution.
*   **Test Environments:** Experiments were conducted in large-scale indoor environments simulated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, using a pre-built 3D dense map. Semantic zones were manually defined, and keyframes were associated with these zones. The tests were run on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8GB of memory, emulating edge deployment. Various VLM models were used to create memory pressure.
*   **Memory Management Results:** The results show that the "Basic + VLM" configuration experienced memory saturation and stalled execution, while the "Semantic + VLM" configuration completed the experiment without issues and maintained stable memory usage. This indicates that semantic zone-based keyframe management reduces memory contention between SLAM and VLM.
*   **Impact on SLAM Performance:** The document begins to analyze how concurrent VLM execution affects SLAM performance, noting substantial degradation in the basic configuration.

nodes.title: Impact of Concurrent SLAM-VLM Execution on VLM Performance
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a semantic zone-based memory management approach for improving the performance of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and Visual-Language Models (VLMs) in resource-constrained edge environments. The main points covered are:

*   **Proposed Memory Management Strategy:** The document introduces a method that controls which keyframes are loaded into memory at runtime based on semantic zones, allowing standard SLAM modules like loop-closure and graph optimization to operate on a subset of the map.
*   **Experimental Setup:** Experiments were conducted in simulated large-scale indoor environments (including a hospital scenario) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8GB of memory. Various edge-scale VLMs were used to stress-test memory contention.
*   **Memory Footprint Reduction:** The semantic zone-based approach significantly reduces memory saturation and avoids out-of-memory (OOM) events and stalled execution compared to the basic, default keyframe loading mechanism, especially when running concurrently with a VLM.
*   **Impact on SLAM Performance:** The proposed method leads to more stable SLAM performance under concurrent VLM execution. It shows improvements in update rate, loop closures, processing time, and localization accuracy (ATE RMSE, RPE RMSE) compared to the basic configuration, which suffers substantial degradation.
*   **Impact on VLM Performance:** The semantic zone-based approach enables the VLM to achieve better token generation speed, lower average latency, and greater operational stability, avoiding the severe latency spikes and freezes observed in the basic configuration.
*   **Discussion and Limitations:** The document discusses how memory saturation can directly impact localization stability. It also identifies limitations, including the manual definition of semantic zones and the use of a simple Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policy, suggesting areas for future improvement like automated segmentation and more advanced eviction strategies.

structure.title: DISCUSSION
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt discusses the impact of concurrent Visual-Language Model (VLM) execution on dense-map utilization performance in Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems, particularly in memory-constrained environments.

The main points covered are:

*   **Performance Degradation of Basic SLAM with Concurrent VLM:** The basic SLAM algorithm experiences significant performance degradation when VLM runs concurrently. This includes reduced update rates, fewer loop closures, drastically increased processing times, and a substantial decrease in localization accuracy (higher ATE RMSE and RPE RMSE). This is attributed to insufficient memory preventing timely keyframe loading.
*   **Improved Stability with Semantic Zone-Based Memory Management:** A proposed semantic zone-based memory management approach demonstrates much more stable performance. It shows only slight increases in update rate and processing time, with significantly less degradation in localization accuracy compared to the basic approach.
*   **VLM Performance Enhancement with Semantic Zones:** The semantic zone-based approach also improves VLM performance. It leads to more consistent token generation speed and lower end-to-end latency, avoiding severe latency spikes and execution stalls that plague the baseline configuration.
*   **Validation and Comparison:** The document presents experimental results (TABLE I, TABLE II, Figure 5, 6, 7) comparing the "Basic + VLM" configuration against the "Semantic + VLM" (proposed) configuration across various metrics like update rate, loop closures, processing time, localization accuracy, VLM token generation throughput, and latency.
*   **Limitations and Future Work:** The authors acknowledge limitations, such as manually defined semantic zones and the use of a simple LRU eviction policy. Future work includes exploring automated zone definition, adaptive strategies, and more advanced eviction policies.
*   **Conclusion:** The semantic zone-based map management scheme is presented as an effective solution for stabilizing dense-map utilization under strict memory constraints, enabling simultaneous operation of memory-intensive SLAM and VLM models while improving overall system robustness and performance.

structure.title: CONCLUSION
structure.summary: The provided document excerpt focuses on evaluating the performance of Visual-Language Models (VLMs) in terms of token generation throughput (TPS) and latency. It presents comparative data in Table II, showing how different VLM models (Qwen3-vl, Qwen3.5, Gemma3) of varying sizes perform under different execution scenarios (basic, relative change, semantic). The document also includes figures (Fig. 5, Fig. 6, Fig. 7) that visualize the probability density and cumulative distribution functions of token generation throughput and latency, as well as their relationship with the robot's position. The conclusion section highlights the benefits of a semantic zone-based map management approach for stabilizing dense-map utilization and improving VLM performance, especially on resource-constrained platforms. Future work directions are also mentioned, including dynamic zone refinement and semantic importance weighting.
